chapter.name: Electromagnetic Induction
chapter.blurb: The chapter shows how a changing magnetic flux induces an emf: the experiments of Faraday and Henry, magnetic flux, Faraday's law for the size of the induced emf and Lenz's law for its direction, with conservation of energy as its basis. It then treats the emf of a conductor moving in a steady field, and the mutual and self-inductance of coils together with the magnetic energy stored in an inductor. It ends with the ac generator, in which a coil rotating in a magnetic field produces an alternating emf.

concepts.name: The experiments of Faraday and Henry
concepts.description: The three coil-and-galvanometer experiments that established electromagnetic induction: a moving magnet, a moving current-carrying coil, and a tapping key in a stationary neighbouring coil.
concepts.idea: An electric current is induced in a coil only while the magnetic field through it is changing, whether the change comes from relative motion or from a changing current nearby.
concepts.rule: Electromagnetic induction is the phenomenon in which electric current is generated by varying magnetic fields; it was demonstrated around 1830 by Michael Faraday in England and Joseph Henry in the USA. Experiment 6.1: a coil C1 is connected to a galvanometer. Pushing the north pole of a bar magnet towards the coil deflects the pointer; the deflection lasts only as long as the magnet moves and is zero when the magnet is held stationary. Pulling the magnet away gives a deflection in the opposite direction. Using the south pole reverses the deflections compared with the north pole for similar movements. Faster motion gives a larger deflection. Moving the coil instead of the magnet gives the same effects, so it is the relative motion that matters. Experiment 6.2: the magnet is replaced by a second coil C2 carrying a steady current from a battery; moving C2 towards or away from C1 (or C1 relative to C2) gives deflections in opposite directions that last only during the motion. Experiment 6.3: both coils are stationary and C2 is connected to a battery through a tapping key. Pressing the key gives a momentary deflection, holding it pressed gives none, and releasing it gives a momentary deflection in the opposite direction, so relative motion is not an absolute requirement. The deflection increases dramatically when an iron rod is inserted into the coils along their axis. A larger deflection in Experiment 6.2 is obtained with a soft iron rod inside C2, a more powerful battery, or more rapid motion; without a galvanometer, a small torch bulb that glows shows the induced current.
concepts.example: Pushing the north pole of a bar magnet into a coil makes the galvanometer pointer kick one way; pulling it out makes it kick the other way; pushing the south pole in gives the opposite kick to the north pole.

concepts.name: Magnetic flux
concepts.description: The definition of magnetic flux through a surface, its dependence on field, area and orientation, and its unit and nature.
concepts.idea: Magnetic flux measures how much magnetic field passes through a surface, and depends on the angle between the field and the area vector.
concepts.rule: Magnetic flux is defined in the same way as electric flux. For a plane of area A in a uniform magnetic field B, Phi_B = B . A = B A cos(theta), where theta is the angle between B and the area vector A (the normal to the plane). The flux is greatest (BA) when the plane is perpendicular to the field (theta = 0), zero when the plane is parallel to the field (theta = 90 degrees), and negative when theta is more than 90 degrees. The definition extends to curved surfaces and non-uniform fields: Phi_B = B1 . dA1 + B2 . dA2 + ... , the sum of B_i . dA_i over all area elements of the surface. The SI unit of magnetic flux is the weber (Wb), equal to tesla metre squared (T m^2). Magnetic flux is a scalar quantity with dimensions [M L^2 T^-2 A^-1].
concepts.example: A square loop of side 30 cm whose area vector makes 60 degrees with a uniform field of 0.4 T has flux 0.4 x 0.09 x cos 60 degrees = 0.018 Wb.

concepts.name: Faraday's law of induction
concepts.description: Faraday's law relating the induced emf to the time rate of change of magnetic flux, for one turn and for N turns, the induced current, and the ways of changing flux.
concepts.idea: An emf is induced in a circuit whenever the magnetic flux through it changes, and its magnitude equals the rate at which the flux changes.
concepts.rule: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction: the magnitude of the induced emf in a circuit is equal to the time rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit, e = -d(Phi_B)/dt. The negative sign indicates the direction of the emf and hence of the current in a closed loop. For a closely wound coil of N turns the change of flux is the same for each turn, so e = -N d(Phi_B)/dt, and the emf can be increased by increasing N. concepts.name: Lenz's law and conservation of energy
concepts.description: Lenz's law for the polarity of the induced emf and the direction of the induced current, its application to magnets and coils and to loops entering or leaving a field, and its basis in conservation of energy.
concepts.idea: The induced current always flows so as to oppose the change in magnetic flux that causes it; otherwise energy would be created from nothing.
concepts.rule: Lenz's law: the polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it. The negative sign in e = -d(Phi_B)/dt represents this. When the north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards a closed coil, the flux through the coil increases and the induced current opposes the increase: it is counter-clockwise as seen by an observer on the side of the magnet, so the face of the coil towards the magnet behaves as a north pole and repels the magnet. When the north pole is withdrawn, the flux decreases; the current is clockwise as seen from the magnet's side, the near face is a south pole and attracts the receding magnet. The induced current opposes the CHANGE in flux, not the flux itself: when flux decreases, the field of the induced current is in the same direction as the original field. With an open circuit an emf is still induced across the open ends, and its direction is found by Lenz's law, but no current flows. Energy: if the current were in the opposite direction, the magnet would be attracted and gain kinetic energy without any energy being spent (a perpetual-motion machine), violating conservation of energy; in the real case the person does work against the repulsion and this energy is dissipated as Joule heating by the induced current. For a planar loop moving into a region of field directed into the page, the flux increases and the current is anticlockwise as seen by the reader; moving out, it is clockwise; no current flows while the loop is wholly inside or wholly outside the field. A loop held stationary between fixed magnets has no induced current however strong the magnets; current cannot be induced by changing electric flux; a rectangular loop leaving a uniform field at constant velocity has a constant emf, whereas a circular loop does not, because its area in the field does not change at a constant rate.
concepts.example: A loop lying in the page is pulled out of a region where the field points into the page: the flux into the page falls, so the induced current is clockwise as seen by the reader, keeping an into-page field inside the loop.

concepts.name: Motional electromotive force
concepts.description: The emf induced across a conductor moving in a uniform, time-independent magnetic field: the expression Blv from Faraday's law and from the Lorentz force, the rotating rod, and the electric field produced by a changing magnetic field.
concepts.idea: Moving a conductor through a steady magnetic field induces an emf, because the magnetic force pushes its free charges along the conductor.
concepts.rule: For a rectangular circuit PQRS in which the arm PQ of length l slides with speed v in a uniform, time-independent field B perpendicular to the plane, the enclosed flux is Phi_B = B l x, and e = -d(B l x)/dt = B l v (with dx/dt = -v when the area decreases). The emf B l v is called motional emf: an emf is produced by moving a conductor, i.e. by changing the area and hence the flux enclosed, instead of varying the field. Lorentz-force explanation: a charge q in the rod moves with speed v in the field B, so the force on it is q v B along the rod; the work done in moving it from one end to the other is W = q v B l, and emf = W/q = B l v. Here l is the length of the conductor that is perpendicular to both the velocity and the field. For a stationary conductor in a changing magnetic field, v = 0, so the force F = q(E + v x B) = qE must come from an electric field: a time-varying magnetic field generates an electric field, whose properties differ from those of fields produced by static charges. A metallic rod of length R rotating with angular speed omega about one end, in a uniform field B normal to the plane of rotation, has emf e = (1/2) B omega R^2 between its ends (from integrating B (omega r) dr, or from B times the rate of change of area of the sector); omega = 2 pi x frequency. For a wheel with several metallic spokes the emf between axle and rim is the same as for one spoke, because the emfs across the spokes are in parallel. 1 G = 10^-4 T. For a loop with a small cut leaving a field region, the emf across the cut is B l v with l the side perpendicular to the velocity, and it lasts while the loop is crossing the edge of the field.
concepts.example: A rod 1 m long rotating at 50 rev/s about one end in a field of 1 T normal to its plane has emf (1/2) x 1 x (2 pi x 50) x 1^2 = 157 V between its ends.

concepts.name: Mutual inductance
concepts.description: Inductance as the ratio of flux linkage to current, and the mutual inductance of two coils: its definition, the formula for two long co-axial solenoids, the equality M12 = M21 and the emf induced by a changing current in a neighbouring coil.
concepts.idea: A changing current in one coil induces an emf in a nearby coil, and the mutual inductance measures how strongly the two coils are linked.
concepts.rule: The flux through a coil is proportional to the current that produces it. For a closely wound coil of N turns the flux linkage is N Phi_B, and N Phi_B is proportional to I; the constant of proportionality is the inductance. Inductance depends only on the geometry and on intrinsic material properties (as capacitance does); it is a scalar with dimensions [M L^2 T^-2 A^-2] (flux divided by current), and its SI unit is the henry (H). Mutual inductance: when a current I2 in coil 2 sets up flux Phi1 through each of the N1 turns of coil 1, N1 Phi1 = M12 I2, where M12 is the mutual inductance (coefficient of mutual induction) of coil 1 with respect to coil 2. For two long co-axial solenoids of the same length l, with n1 and n2 turns per unit length and inner radius r1: the field of the outer solenoid is mu0 n2 I2, the flux linkage with the inner one is (n1 l)(pi r1^2)(mu0 n2 I2), so M12 = mu0 n1 n2 pi r1^2 l; edge effects are neglected because the solenoids are long (l much greater than r2). In the reverse case the flux of the inner solenoid is confined inside it, so the area is again pi r1^2 and M21 = mu0 n1 n2 pi r1^2 l. Thus M12 = M21 = M, a relation that is far more general and is useful when one of the two calculations is extremely difficult (a short coil well inside a long solenoid). With a medium of relative permeability mu_r, M = mu_r mu0 n1 n2 pi r1^2 l. The mutual inductance of a pair of coils depends on their separation and relative orientation. For a small coil of radius r1 at the centre of a large co-axial coil of radius r2 (r1 much less than r2), M = mu0 pi r1^2 / (2 r2). For a changing current, e1 = -M dI2/dt: the emf depends on the rate of change of current and on M. Change of flux linkage = M x (change of current).
concepts.example: A pair of coils has M = 1.5 H; when the current in one changes from 0 to 20 A, the flux linkage with the other changes by 1.5 x 20 = 30 Wb.

Because M12 = M21, this gives the same mutual inductance.
s: Judgement - flux linkage with the long solenoid is extremely difficult to calculate (non-uniform field)
Better plan - current in the long solenoid, flux linkage of the short coil; valid since M12 = M21

concepts.name: Self-inductance and magnetic energy
concepts.description: Self-induction and the back emf, the self-inductance of a long solenoid, and the magnetic energy (1/2) L I^2 stored in an inductor, including the energy per unit volume of a magnetic field.
concepts.idea: A coil resists any change in its own current, and the work done against this back emf is stored as magnetic energy.
concepts.rule: Self-induction is the induction of an emf in a single isolated coil due to the change of flux through it caused by varying the current in the same coil. The flux linkage is proportional to the current: N Phi_B = L I, where L is the self-inductance (coefficient of self-induction). When the current varies, e = -L dI/dt, so the self-induced emf always opposes any change (increase or decrease) of current; it is called the back emf. For a long solenoid of cross-sectional area A and length l with n turns per unit length, B = mu0 n I, the flux linkage is (n l)(mu0 n I)(A), and L = mu0 n^2 A l; with a core of relative permeability mu_r (for example soft iron), L = mu_r mu0 n^2 A l. L depends on the geometry and on the permeability of the medium, not on the current. Self-inductance plays the role of inertia: it is the electromagnetic analogue of mass. Work must be done against the back emf to establish a current: dW/dt = |e| I = L I dI/dt, so the energy required to build up a current I is W = (1/2) L I^2, stored as magnetic potential energy; this resembles (1/2) m v^2, with L analogous to m. For a solenoid the energy is U = B^2 A l / (2 mu0), so the magnetic energy per unit volume is u = B^2 / (2 mu0), to be compared with the electrostatic energy density (1/2) epsilon0 E^2: in both, the energy is proportional to the square of the field. With currents in two nearby coils, e1 = -L1 dI1/dt - M12 dI2/dt.
concepts.example: The current in a circuit falls from 5.0 A to 0 in 0.1 s and the average induced emf is 200 V, so L = 200 x 0.1 / 5.0 = 4 H.

questions.a: For a long solenoid B = mu0 n I, so I = B / (mu0 n), and L = mu0 n^2 A l. U = (1/2) L I^2 = (1/2)(mu0 n^2 A l)(B / (mu0 n))^2 = B^2 A l / (2 mu0). In both cases the energy density is proportional to the square of the field strength.
s: Substitute I = B / (mu0 n) and L = mu0 n^2 A l to get U = B^2 A l / (2 mu0)
Energy per unit volume u = B^2 / (2 mu0)
Comparison with (1/2) epsilon0 E^2 - both proportional to the square of the field

concepts.name: The ac generator
concepts.description: The construction and working of a simple ac generator, the expression for the alternating emf of a coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field, and the sources of mechanical energy in commercial generators.
concepts.idea: Rotating a coil in a magnetic field changes the flux through it periodically, giving an emf that alternates in sign.
concepts.rule: An ac generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction. A coil (the armature) mounted on a rotor shaft is rotated mechanically in a uniform magnetic field, about an axis perpendicular to the field; its ends are connected to the external circuit by slip rings and brushes. As the coil rotates, the effective area facing the field is A cos(theta), where theta is the angle between the area vector A and B. With constant angular speed omega and theta = 0 at t = 0, theta = omega t and the flux through each turn is Phi_B = B A cos(omega t). By Faraday's law, e = -N d(Phi_B)/dt = N B A omega sin(omega t) = e0 sin(omega t), where e0 = N B A omega is the maximum emf, reached when sin(omega t) = +1 or -1, i.e. theta = 90 or 270 degrees (plane of the coil parallel to the field), where the flux is changing fastest. The emf is zero when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field (theta = 0, 180 degrees). Since omega = 2 pi x (frequency of revolution), e = e0 sin(2 pi (frequency) t). The polarity of the emf changes with time, so the current changes direction periodically and is called alternating current (ac). In commercial generators the mechanical energy comes from water falling from a height (hydro-electric), from steam at high pressure produced using coal or other sources (thermal), or from nuclear fuel (nuclear power generators). In most generators the coils are held stationary and the electromagnets are rotated. The frequency of rotation is 50 Hz in India and 60 Hz in certain countries such as the USA.
concepts.example: A 50-turn coil of area 0.04 m^2 rotating at 10 revolutions per second (omega = 62.8 rad/s) in a field of 0.2 T has maximum emf N B A omega = 50 x 0.2 x 0.04 x 62.8 = 25.1 V.

N = 100 turns from e0 = N B A omega
